Business.q: Which of these is NOT a business?
Business.right: A family cooking dinner for itself at home
wrong: A teenager who sells custom phone cases to classmates through an online store
Selling goods for money makes it a business.
A barber who cuts hair for pay
Selling a service makes it a business.
An app that sells movie tickets
Business.exp: A business produces and distributes goods or services for customers; cooking for yourself isn't selling anything.

Business.q: A company sells only through its website to customers in 40 countries. What does this show?
Business.right: Businesses can be virtual and global
wrong: It isn't really a business because it doesn't have a physical store location
Business.exp: Businesses can serve customers face to face or virtually, locally or globally.

Goods.q: A concert venue sells T-shirts and also charges for coat check. Which is the good?
wrong: The coat check, because customers get their coats back in their hands
Coat check is work done for you: a service.
Goods.exp: Goods are tangible things you can own.

Goods.q: A ski resort rents helmets and sells lessons. Which statement is correct?
Goods.right: The helmet is a good; the lesson is a service
wrong: Both are services, since customers don't keep the helmet after renting it
The helmet is still a tangible item.
A lesson is work done for you.
Goods.exp: Goods are tangible items; services are work performed for pay.

Services.q: Which of these is a service?
wrong: A box of cereal sold at a grocery store to a family with young children
Services.exp: Services are work performed for payment.

Services.q: A homeowner hires a company to clean the air conditioner and buys a filter from it. Which is the service?
wrong: The filter, because the homeowner needs it to keep the system working well
The filter is tangible: a good.
The cleaning is work done for pay.
Services.exp: Cleaning is work performed for payment; the filter is a good.

Profit.q: A bakery earns $18,000 in revenue and pays $17,000 in total costs. What is its profit?
wrong: $18,000, since that is all of the money the bakery collected from its customers

Profit.q: A business has $1.2 million in revenue and $1.35 million in costs. Which statement is correct?
Profit.right: It has revenue but a $150,000 loss
wrong: It earned $150,000 in profit, since the gap between revenue and costs is positive
Costs are higher, so it's a loss.
It can still create value for customers.
Profit.exp: When costs exceed revenue, there is a loss, not a profit.

Customer.q: A school district signs a contract to buy lunches; students choose whether to eat them. Who is the customer?
wrong: The students, because they are the ones who decide each day whether to eat the meals
Customer.exp: The customer pays and makes the buying decision.

Customer.q: A parent buys a meal subscription for a college student, who picks and eats the meals. Which role does the parent play?
wrong: Consumer, since the parent is the one spending money on the meal subscription
The consumer is the one who uses it.
Customer.exp: The parent pays: customer. The student uses: consumer.

Consumer.q: A delivery company buys e-bikes for its couriers to ride. Who is the consumer?
Consumer.right: The couriers who ride the bikes
wrong: The delivery company, because it paid for the bikes and signed the purchase contract
Consumer.exp: The consumer is the person who uses the product.

Consumer.q: A museum buys audio guides that visitors use on tours. Which is correct?
Consumer.right: The museum is the customer; visitors are consumers
wrong: The visitors are the customers, because they physically hold the devices on tours
They use them but didn't buy them.
The museum paid but doesn't use them.

Need.q: Which purchase is best classified as a need?
wrong: Premium imported chocolates bought for the family to enjoy after dinner
Need.exp: Needs are essential for survival: food, water, shelter, basic healthcare.

Need.q: A person with no place to live rents a small apartment. How is the apartment classified?
wrong: A want, because the person could choose a nicer apartment in a better area instead
Rent is for housing, a need.

Want.q: A commuter who already owns a reliable watch buys a luxury watch for prestige. What is the luxury watch?
wrong: A need, because everyone has to know the time to get to work on schedule
He already has a working watch.
Want.exp: Wants improve quality of life but aren't necessary.

Want.q: Why would a business care whether its product meets a need or a want?
Want.right: It shapes how the product is designed and marketed
wrong: Because businesses are not allowed by law to sell anything that is only a want
Wants are sold all the time.
Want.exp: Businesses consider customers' problems, needs and wants when designing and marketing products.

Problem-solution fit.q: Photographers say late payments waste time. A startup's reminder tool takes so long to set up that they stop using it. What does this show?
Problem-solution fit.right: The problem is real but the fit is weak
wrong: The startup has shown strong problem-solution fit because the problem it found is real
A real problem isn't enough; the solution must work.
Problem-solution fit.exp: Problem-solution fit needs a real problem AND a solution that effectively solves it.

Problem-solution fit.q: Which evidence best shows problem-solution fit?
Problem-solution fit.right: Customers keep using it because it solves their problem
wrong: Managers believe customers might dislike the problem the product is meant to solve
Problem-solution fit.exp: Repeated use because it works is strong evidence of fit.

Value creation.q: A hotel turns unused lobby space into work pods, saving travelers' time. What is the time saved?
wrong: Value capture, since the hotel benefits when guests use the new work pods
Capture is the money the hotel earns.
Value creation.exp: Benefits to customers are value creation.

Value creation.q: A free app saves students hours each week but earns no money. Which is true?
Value creation.right: It creates value but captures little
wrong: It cannot create any value because it doesn't charge its users anything
Its users' time savings are its profit
Value creation.exp: Value creation can happen without value capture.

Value capture.q: An e-bike costs $800 to make and sells for $1,800. How much value does the company capture per bike?
wrong: $1,800, which is the full price that customers pay for each of the bikes

Value capture.q: A note app is popular for free; it then charges for a pro tier. What does charging represent?
wrong: Value creation, because users who pay for the pro tier get more storage space
The charge is the business taking value.
Value capture.exp: Charging for value delivered is value capture.

Value proposition.q: "Cut picking errors and find inventory faster with real-time shelf tracking." What is this?
wrong: A mission statement, since it explains what the company does for its customers
A mission statement describes the company, not why to choose a product.
Value proposition.exp: It says how the product solves a problem and why to choose it.

Value proposition.q: How does a value proposition differ from problem-solution fit?
Value proposition.right: One communicates the value; the other is whether it works
wrong: A value proposition measures profit, while problem-solution fit measures revenue
A value proposition identifies the consumer
Value proposition.exp: A value proposition explains why to choose a product; problem-solution fit is whether it actually solves the problem.

Product-market fit.q: A survey finds 48% of users would be "very disappointed" if an app disappeared. By your study guide's test, what does this suggest?
wrong: Product failure, because more than half of the users would not be disappointed at all
Product-market fit.exp: Your study guide: at least 40% "very disappointed" signals product-market fit.

Product-market fit.q: Which is the best evidence that a product has product-market fit, not just problem-solution fit?
Product-market fit.right: Enough customers buy it to make the business viable
wrong: The product solves the problem it was designed for in early lab tests by engineers
Product-market fit.exp: Product-market fit means enough demand for the business to be viable.

Build-measure-learn.q: A shoe startup launches a small online store, studies what customers order and return, then changes its selection. Which cycle is this?
wrong: The product life cycle, which follows sales through introduction, growth and decline
That's about sales stages, not testing.
Build-measure-learn.exp: Launch, gather feedback, refine: build-measure-learn (like Zappos).

Build-measure-learn.q: Why do businesses use build-measure-learn instead of perfecting a product first?
Build-measure-learn.right: Feedback shows what to fix before investing more
wrong: It guarantees that the product will be profitable from the very first day
It replaces the need for a product
Build-measure-learn.exp: Launching, measuring and learning lets a business improve with real feedback.

Minimum viable product (MVP).q: A software company releases a stripped-down app with only its core feature to test demand. What is it?
wrong: A minimum marketable product, since it is ready to sell to a large group of customers
An MMP has grown beyond the test version.
Minimum viable product (MVP).exp: An MVP is the simplest working version used to test demand.

Minimum viable product (MVP).q: A startup tests its MVP and customers keep asking for one missing feature. What should it most likely do?
Minimum viable product (MVP).right: Use the feedback to improve the product
wrong: Stop testing, because an MVP is meant to be the final version of the product
Minimum viable product (MVP).exp: MVPs exist to gather feedback and improve.

Minimum marketable product (MMP).q: An app has moved past its first test version and is ready for a larger customer group. What is it now?
wrong: An MVP, because every product stays an MVP until the company earns its first profit
It has evolved beyond the MVP.
Minimum marketable product (MMP).exp: MMP: evolved beyond the MVP and ready for a larger segment.

Minimum marketable product (MMP).q: Put these in order: MMP, MVP, idea.
wrong: MMP → MVP → idea, starting from the most complete version and working backward
The MVP comes before the MMP.
Minimum marketable product (MMP).exp: A product starts as an idea, is tested as an MVP, then grows into an MMP.

Business Canvas.q: Why does your teacher say the six Business Canvas lenses matter beyond the class project?
Business Canvas.right: They are how you analyze case studies on the exam
wrong: They are the six PESTEL factors that every business must track in its environment
They are the six departments of every corporation
Business Canvas.exp: The six lenses are the same strategic lenses used for case studies.

Business Canvas.q: Which list names the six lenses?
Business Canvas.right: Customer, Product, Market, Finance, Operations, Organization
wrong: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal
Product, Price, Place, Promotion, People, Profit
Sales, R&D, Operations, Accounting, Finance, HR
Business Canvas.exp: Customer, Product, Market, Finance, Operations, Organization.

Customer lens.q: A pet-care company decides whether to serve frequent travelers or owners of elderly pets. Which lens?
wrong: Market, because it is studying the different groups of people who own pets
Market is about competitors and alternatives.
Customer lens.exp: Choosing who to serve is the Customer lens.

Customer lens.q: A company studies whether students or working adults are more frustrated by a scheduling problem. Which lens?
wrong: Product, because the company will eventually build a scheduling product for them
This step is about who has the problem.
Customer lens.exp: Who has the problem is the Customer lens.

Product lens.q: After choosing its customers, a company decides between video check-ins and GPS walk reports. Which lens?
wrong: Customer, because the features are chosen to please the customers it selected
Choosing features is the Product lens.
Product lens.exp: Deciding features and how they create value is the Product lens.

Product lens.q: A restaurant considers adding mobile ordering to improve its service. Which lens?
wrong: Operations, because mobile ordering changes how the kitchen receives each order
The focus is improving what customers get.
Product lens.exp: Improving the offering is the Product lens.

Market lens.q: A company compares kennels, pet sitters and other apps that customers might use instead. Which lens?
wrong: Customer, because the company is looking at what its customers do today
Comparing alternatives is the Market lens.
Market lens.exp: The competitive environment and alternatives are the Market lens.

Market lens.q: Managers ask how crowded the field of educational apps is. Which lens?
wrong: Product, because the company needs to decide what features its own app should have
Not about who the customer is.

Finance lens.q: A retailer estimates sales, rent and payroll for a second location. Which lens?
wrong: Operations, because opening a store changes how products get to the customers
The question is whether it can be profitable.
Finance lens.exp: Revenue and costs are the Finance lens.

Finance lens.q: Management sets profit-margin goals and adjusts prices to meet them. Which lens?
wrong: Product, since prices are part of what the customer sees when they buy
Finance lens.exp: Managing revenue, costs and profit is Finance.

Operations lens.q: A furniture maker maps each step from design approval to delivery to remove bottlenecks. Which lens?
wrong: Organization, because the company is deciding which team handles each part of the work
This is about the production process.
Operations lens.exp: How a product is produced and delivered is Operations.

Operations lens.q: A small company plans how to handle extra holiday orders. Which lens?
wrong: Finance, because extra holiday orders will bring in more revenue for the company
Handling orders is a process question.

Organization lens.q: A consulting firm grows to 150 people and decides who reports to whom. Which lens?
wrong: Operations, because the firm needs to decide how the work gets done each day
Organization lens.exp: People, structure and roles are the Organization lens.

Organization lens.q: A business considers hiring a regional manager to oversee several stores. Which lens?
wrong: Customer, because a regional manager would help keep customers happy in each store

Market.q: Which of these is NOT a market?
Market.right: A household where parents assign chores
wrong: An app store where developers sell games to people with smartphones around the world
A virtual marketplace is a market.
Market.exp: A market is any physical or virtual space where buyers and sellers exchange.

Market.q: An online platform lets students buy and sell used textbooks. What makes it a market?
Market.right: Buyers and sellers interact to exchange
wrong: It is owned by a corporation that sells shares of stock to investors
Prices are set by the government
Not required, and not true here.
Market.exp: Interaction of buyers and sellers is what makes a market.

Voluntary exchange.q: A shopper pays $40 for a backpack she values more than $40; the seller would rather have the $40. What is this?
wrong: Collusion, since both the buyer and the seller agreed on the price ahead of time
Voluntary exchange.exp: Both sides trade willingly because each expects to be better off.

Voluntary exchange.q: Which situation is NOT voluntary exchange?
Voluntary exchange.right: A law requires every household to buy a service
wrong: A customer buys coffee because she'd rather have the coffee than keep her $5
A store sells shoes to a willing buyer
A student sells an old bike to a friend
Voluntary exchange.exp: Being forced to buy isn't voluntary.

Equilibrium price.q: At $90, buyers want 5,000 sneakers and sellers offer 5,000. What is $90?
wrong: A surplus price, because sellers are producing more sneakers than buyers want
Equilibrium price.exp: Where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is equilibrium.

Equilibrium price.q: Who sets the price in a competitive market?
wrong: The seller alone, based on how much profit it wants to earn on each sale
Equilibrium price.exp: In competitive markets, the interaction of buyers and sellers sets the price.

Shortage.q: At the current price, fans want 1,800 concert tickets but only 1,200 are offered. What is likely?
Shortage.right: A shortage pushes the price up
wrong: A surplus pushes the price down as sellers compete for the buyers that remain
Buyers want more than is offered.
Shortage.exp: Quantity demanded > supplied is a shortage; buyers compete and the price rises.

Shortage.q: Fresh strawberries sell out faster than shipments arrive. What do stores face?
wrong: A surplus, because the farm keeps harvesting more strawberries than usual
Shortage.exp: Buyers want more than is available.

Surplus.q: At $90, buyers want 5,000 pairs of sneakers but sellers offer 7,500. What happens?
wrong: A shortage; the price rises because buyers compete for the limited sneakers
Sellers offer more than buyers want.
The government sets a new price
Surplus.exp: Quantity supplied > demanded is a surplus; sellers compete and the price falls.

Surplus.q: As the price falls during a surplus, what happens?
Surplus.right: Buyers want more and sellers offer less
wrong: Buyers want less and sellers offer more, making the surplus even bigger
Sellers offer less at a lower price.
Surplus.exp: A falling price raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied until the surplus disappears.

Competitive advantage.q: A local coffee shop adds mobile ordering, faster service and rewards while rivals sell similar coffee at similar prices. What is it doing?
Competitive advantage.right: Building a competitive advantage through experience
wrong: Creating a legal barrier to entry that stops new coffee shops from opening nearby
Competitive advantage.exp: Differentiating the customer experience is a source of competitive advantage.

Competitive advantage.q: 72% of a smartwatch maker's buyers say they chose it for exclusive features, and only 14% for price. What is its main advantage?
Competitive advantage.right: Unique features customers will pay more for
wrong: Lower production costs than every rival, which lets it sell at the lowest price
Price isn't why most people buy.
Competitive advantage.exp: Its advantage is differentiation through features.

Commodities.q: A tomato farmer sells tomatoes nearly identical to hundreds of other farms. What is the best path to an advantage?
wrong: Charging much more, since customers can't find tomatoes anywhere else in town
Running national TV ads about its tomatoes' brand
Branding works poorly for identical products.
Commodities.exp: With commodities, efficiency and low cost are the main advantage.

Commodities.q: Which product is the best example of a commodity?
wrong: A smartphone with a patented camera that no other brand is allowed to use
Commodities.exp: Commodities are nearly identical regardless of seller.

Differentiated products.q: Gyms in a city compete on equipment, classes, atmosphere and trainers. What are they selling?
wrong: Commodities, because every gym basically offers a place to exercise and lift weights
Differentiated products.exp: Products with features that set them apart are differentiated.

Differentiated products.q: Why can a lighting company with a patented "Smart-Dim" feature charge $500 for a unit that costs $150 to make?
wrong: Its customers are consumers who don't care how much they pay for their lighting
The developers are customers who do care.
Prices in competitive markets equal production costs
Voluntary exchange benefits only the seller
Differentiated products.exp: A unique product reduces the pull of rival products.

Low-cost strategy.q: Walmart and Costco often compete by doing what?
Low-cost strategy.right: Lowering costs and offering lower prices
wrong: Offering the most exclusive luxury products in the market at premium prices
Low-cost strategy.exp: Your notes list Walmart and Costco as low-cost competitors.

Low-cost strategy.q: Which business is most likely to rely on a low-cost strategy?
wrong: A luxury watchmaker that hand-assembles each watch for collectors
Low-cost strategy.exp: Identical products push firms toward low-cost competition.

Market share.q: ActiveTech sells 8.0 million watches in a market of 20 million. What is its market share?
wrong: 8%, since ActiveTech sold eight million of the watches during the year

Market share.q: Total smartwatch sales rise 8% next year but Pulse sells the same 3.6 million watches. What happens to Pulse's market share?
wrong: It rises, because the whole market for smartwatches is growing larger
Pulse's slice stays the same size while the pie grows.
Market share.exp: Same sales in a bigger market means a smaller share.

Barriers to entry.q: Two of three new smartwatch startups quit after failing to raise enough money for product development. What is discouraging entry?
Barriers to entry.right: The high cost of developing comparable technology
wrong: Strong demand for smartwatches, which is expected to grow next year
Customers having many brands to choose from
Barriers to entry.exp: Large development costs are a barrier to entry.

Barriers to entry.q: Why do barriers to entry help existing firms?
wrong: They force existing firms to lower prices to match every new competitor that arrives
Barriers to entry.exp: Barriers protect existing firms from new rivals.

High startup costs.q: A new airline must spend billions on planes, gates and safety approvals before its first flight. What is this?
wrong: Product differentiation, because every airline offers a different flying experience
The point is the cost of entering.
High startup costs.exp: Huge upfront costs are a barrier to entry.

High startup costs.q: Which industry most likely has the highest startup-cost barrier?
wrong: Opening a dog-walking service in a neighborhood with lots of dog owners
High startup costs.exp: Airlines require billions before carrying a passenger.

Control of resources.q: A company signs exclusive contracts with every major supplier of a special glass. A startup can't find glass. What blocks the startup?
Control of resources.right: A barrier from control of resources
wrong: Lack of problem-solution fit, since the startup's lights don't solve any problem
Control of resources.exp: Locking up key suppliers is a barrier to entry.

Control of resources.q: FreshLock signs an exclusive deal with the only domestic supplier of a special seal material. What does this create?
wrong: A shortage of food-storage containers that raises prices across the whole industry
Control of resources.exp: Controlling a key input keeps rivals out.

Patent.q: A drug company receives a patent on a new medicine. What does it most directly do?
Patent.right: Stops rivals from making it for a time
wrong: Guarantees that patients and doctors will choose the drug over all alternatives
Patent.exp: A patent gives temporary exclusive rights to an invention.

Patent.q: If a water-filter startup gets a patent before launch, what is most likely in the first few years?
wrong: It becomes the only company allowed to sell any household water product at all
A patent covers its own invention only.
It can charge any price without affecting demand
It never needs to improve the product
Patent.exp: Patents protect the specific invention for a limited time.

Trademark.q: A company registers its sunburst logo with the government. What protection is this?
wrong: A patent, since the logo was invented by the company's own design team
Copyright protects creative works like books.
Trademark.exp: Trademarks protect brand names and logos.

Trademark.q: Why might a rival be stopped from using a nearly identical swoosh logo?
wrong: The original company owns a patent on athletic shoes as an invention

Copyright.q: A game studio's code and music are protected from copying. Which protection covers creative works like these?
wrong: Patent, because video games are new inventions that took years to develop
Patents cover inventions; creative works are copyrighted.

Copyright.q: Which of these is protected by copyright, not a patent?
wrong: A new kind of engine invented by a car company's engineering team

Limit pricing.q: A dominant firm keeps prices low enough that no newcomer could earn a profit. What is this?
wrong: Penetration pricing, since the firm is keeping its prices low to win market share
Penetration is a newcomer's low entry price.
Limit pricing.exp: Low prices that block profitable entry are limit pricing.

Limit pricing.q: Why is limit pricing listed as a barrier to entry?
wrong: It forces the government to give the company a patent on its low prices
Limit pricing.exp: Very low prices make entry unprofitable.

Vertical integration.q: Apple designs its chips, software and phones and runs its own stores. What is this?
wrong: Outsourcing, because Apple hires other firms to handle each part of the process
Vertical integration.exp: Controlling several stages of production and distribution is vertical integration.

Vertical integration.q: A coffee chain buys its own farms and roasting plants. What advantage might this give?
Vertical integration.right: More control over supply and quality
wrong: It removes all competition from the coffee market for the next ten years
It turns coffee into a commodity
Vertical integration.exp: Owning more stages gives control over supply, quality and costs.

Perfect competition.q: Hundreds of farms sell identical wheat, have no control over price and can enter easily. Which structure?
wrong: Oligopoly, because wheat farms often sell to a few very large food companies
Perfect competition.exp: Many firms, identical products, no price control: perfect competition.

Perfect competition.q: Why is cost efficiency most important in perfect competition?
Perfect competition.right: Firms can't raise prices, so they must cut costs
wrong: Firms can charge whatever they like because their product is unique

Monopolistic competition.q: Many restaurants compete with different menus, atmospheres and service. Which structure?
wrong: Perfect competition, since there are so many restaurants that no one controls price
Monopolistic competition.exp: Many firms with differentiated products: monopolistic competition.

Monopolistic competition.right: Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products
wrong: Oligopoly: many small firms selling identical products with no barriers

Oligopoly.q: Four airlines carry nearly all passengers, and starting an airline costs billions. Which structure?
wrong: Monopolistic competition, because each airline offers a slightly different experience
A few dominant firms with high barriers is oligopoly.
Oligopoly.exp: A few large firms and high barriers: oligopoly.

Oligopoly.q: Which feature best separates an oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
Oligopoly.right: A few large firms dominate behind high barriers
wrong: Firms in the market sell products to consumers and try to earn a profit
Oligopoly.exp: Few dominant firms and significant barriers mark an oligopoly.

Monopoly.q: A city lets one company provide water because building rival pipe systems would be wasteful. Which structure?
wrong: Oligopoly, since a few water companies often serve the larger cities nearby
Only one firm is allowed here.
Monopoly.exp: One firm with no close substitutes: monopoly (a local utility).

Monopoly.q: If new firms were allowed to enter a monopoly market, what would most likely happen?
Monopoly.right: Prices and the monopolist's profits would fall
wrong: Prices would rise because the new firms would add to the total costs of the market
Monopoly.exp: More competition lowers prices and profits.

Price taker.q: A wheat farmer sets a price above the market price. What happens to her sales?
wrong: They rise, because a higher price makes buyers think the wheat is better quality
Price taker.exp: Buyers get identical wheat elsewhere at the market price.

Price taker.q: Which firm is most likely a price taker?
Price taker.right: One of hundreds of corn farms
wrong: The only electric company in a city, which is allowed to serve every household
Price taker.exp: Firms in perfect competition are price takers.

Collusion.q: Several airlines secretly agree to charge the same high fare. What is this?
wrong: Competitive pricing, since all of the airlines ended up charging the same fare
Collusion.exp: Agreeing on prices instead of competing is collusion.

Collusion.q: Why is collusion hard to keep up in a market with many firms?
Collusion.right: Each firm can gain by cheating with lower prices
wrong: The government requires all firms in a market to charge exactly the same price
Collusion.exp: With many firms and low barriers, coordination is hard and cheating pays.

Business environment.q: Which of these is part of a business's environment rather than its own decision?
wrong: The company's decision to hire an experienced regional manager for new stores
A new product the company designs
Business environment.exp: The business environment is external factors a business can't control.

Business environment.q: Why do businesses watch their environment closely?
Business environment.right: To spot opportunities and risks early
wrong: To control the factors so that competitors cannot use them to their advantage
Business environment.exp: Recognizing changes helps businesses foresee opportunities, anticipate risks and decide where to operate.

PESTEL.q: What is the main purpose of a PESTEL analysis?
PESTEL.right: To judge how outside changes may affect decisions
wrong: To identify the internal strengths that set the company apart from its competitors
To predict which strategy will be most profitable
Too strong; it informs, doesn't predict.
To decide whether to rewrite the mission statement
PESTEL.exp: PESTEL helps managers evaluate how external changes may affect future decisions.

PESTEL.q: A restaurant chain lists: a minimum-wage increase, a high-protein diet trend, a new delivery app and a stricter labeling law. What is it doing?
wrong: A market research survey that collects opinions from the restaurant's own customers
These are external factors, not survey results.

Viability.q: Which question is about a business's viability?
Viability.right: Can it keep operating successfully over time?
wrong: Which department should be in charge of hiring the new employees next year?
What color should the logo be?
Viability.exp: Viability is the ability to operate successfully and sustainably.

Viability.q: A region's PESTEL factors fit a farm-to-table restaurant: health-conscious residents, local farms, friendly rules. What does this most improve?
wrong: The restaurant's legal liability, since owners become personally responsible for debts
Viability.exp: Businesses enter markets where PESTEL factors align with their model.

Internal vs. external.q: A restaurant chain develops a food-prep system that cuts waste by 15%. Which statement is true?
Internal vs. external.right: It is not part of a PESTEL analysis
wrong: It is a technological PESTEL factor, since it is new technology that changes costs
It's the company's own innovation, not an outside force.
Internal vs. external.exp: PESTEL covers external forces; a firm's own invention is internal.

Internal vs. external.q: Tesla develops better battery cells. Why isn't this a technological PESTEL factor for Tesla?
Internal vs. external.right: It's Tesla's own innovation, not an outside force
wrong: Because batteries are an environmental factor, since they affect carbon emissions
Internal vs. external.exp: PESTEL technology means outside tech changes, not a firm's own R&D.

Opportunity or threat.q: Automation robots become available to restaurants. For a small restaurant, this is best described as:
Opportunity or threat.right: Both an opportunity and a risk
wrong: Only a threat, because robots always cost more than workers in every situation
It can lower labor costs too.
High upfront costs are a risk.
Opportunity or threat.exp: Automation can cut labor costs but has high upfront costs that favor big firms.

Opportunity or threat.q: Interest rates rise from 4% to 7% just as an e-bike company plans to borrow $120 million. This factor is mainly:
wrong: A social opportunity, since people will want more e-bikes as interest rates rise
Interest rates are economic and raise borrowing costs.
Opportunity or threat.exp: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs, an economic obstacle.

Political factors.q: A government offers a tax credit to anyone who installs solar panels. Which PESTEL factor?
wrong: Economic, because the tax credit puts more money back into homeowners' pockets
Solar is tech, but the credit is policy.
Political factors.exp: Government policies and subsidies are political factors.

Political factors.q: Several states approve tax credits for electric-bike purchases. What effect is most likely?
wrong: Borrowing costs rise for e-bike makers, making it harder to build new factories

Tariff.q: The U.S. adds a tax on imported steel. What is this, and who is most hurt?
Tariff.right: A tariff; firms that buy imported steel
wrong: A subsidy; foreign steel makers who sell to American companies
A tariff; American consumers who don't buy steel
Firms using imported steel pay more.
Tariff.exp: A tariff is a tax on imports; buyers of imports pay more.

Tariff.q: Which PESTEL category does a tariff belong to?
wrong: Economic, since a tariff changes the price that businesses pay for imported goods
Tariff.exp: Trade policies like tariffs are political factors.

Economic factors.q: Why might a business find a market unattractive during high inflation?
Economic factors.right: Customers can afford to buy less
wrong: Inflation leads directly to stricter employment laws that protect workers
Economic factors.exp: Economic factors like inflation reduce spending power.

Economic factors.q: An ice cream shop sees sales drop as household incomes fall. Which factor?
wrong: Social, because people are changing their eating habits toward healthier desserts
Economic factors.exp: Income and spending are economic factors.

Recession.q: During a recession, which business is most likely to see sales fall?
wrong: A grocery store selling basic foods that families must buy every single week
Recession.exp: In a decline, people cut wants like luxury travel first.

Recession.q: Economic activity declines for several months. What is this called?
wrong: Inflation, which means that the prices of most goods are rising quickly
Recession.exp: A recession is a decline in economic activity.

Social factors.q: Consumers increasingly prefer environmentally friendly transportation. Your practice test labels this which way for an e-bike maker?
wrong: A legal requirement that forces all consumers to buy electric bicycles instead of cars
It's a preference, not a law.

Social factors.q: Consumers are buying more high-protein, low-carb meals. Which PESTEL factor is this?
wrong: Economic, because people are spending more money on food in restaurants
Social factors.exp: Lifestyle and health trends are social factors.

Demographics.q: A region's population is getting older. For a company making mobility scooters, this is:
wrong: A legal threat, because older customers are protected by consumer protection laws
Demographics.exp: Age is a demographic characteristic, a social factor.

wrong: Interest in outdoor yoga, which a company might learn from social media posts
Demographics.exp: Demographics are statistical traits: age, income, education, location.

Technological factors.q: A new food-delivery platform expands throughout a region. For a restaurant chain this is:
wrong: A social factor, because people are changing how they like to eat their meals
Technological factors.exp: New digital platforms available to firms are technological factors.

Technological factors.q: Which pair is one social and one technological factor?
Technological factors.right: Interest in high-protein meals; a new delivery platform
wrong: A higher minimum wage and a stricter food-labeling law passed by the state
A new prep system and a new manager
A delivery platform and a prep system
Technological factors.exp: Diet trends are social; a new outside platform is technological.

Automation.q: A burger robot can flip patties with little human labor. Which term describes this?
wrong: Outsourcing, because the restaurant hires another company to do the cooking
No outside firm does the work.
Automation.exp: Automation uses technology to do tasks with minimal labor.

Automation.q: Why can automation give large firms an advantage over small ones?
Automation.right: Large firms can afford the high upfront cost
wrong: Small firms are not allowed by law to buy automated equipment for their kitchens
Automation only works in big buildings
Automation.exp: High upfront costs are easier for big firms.

Environmental factors.q: A heat wave boosts ice cream sales. Which factor is this?
wrong: Economic, because the shop earns more revenue when the weather is hot
Environmental factors.exp: Climate and weather are environmental factors.

Environmental factors.q: Severe flooding closes highways between farm warehouses and distributors. Which factor is this?
wrong: Political, because the government decides when to close and reopen the highways
The cause is a natural disaster.

Legal factors.q: New federal rules require battery recycling programs next year. For an e-bike maker this is:
Legal factors.right: A legal factor that raises costs
wrong: A social factor that increases demand, because customers like recycling programs
It's a law that adds compliance costs.
Legal factors.exp: Laws a business must follow are legal factors.

Legal factors.q: Several states pass strict labeling laws for meat-alternative products. How does this affect the maker?
wrong: It speeds up product innovation, since companies must invent new kinds of labels
Legal factors.exp: Legal factors like labeling rules raise costs and can make a market less attractive.

Political vs. legal.q: Which is a POLITICAL factor rather than a legal one?
Political vs. legal.right: A government's new policy to subsidize clean energy
wrong: A state law requiring restaurants to post calorie counts on every menu item
Political vs. legal.exp: Policy priorities are political; specific laws are legal.

Political vs. legal.q: A new law requires food handlers to follow strict sanitation steps. Which factor?
wrong: Political, because the law was passed by elected officials in the government
The law a business must follow is legal.
Political vs. legal.exp: Specific laws and regulations are legal factors.

Entrepreneur.q: Maya leaves a job to start a mobile pet-grooming business with her own savings. What makes her an entrepreneur?
Entrepreneur.right: She bears the risk of a new business
wrong: She works for a large corporation that pays her a steady salary and benefits
She left that to take a risk.
Entrepreneur.exp: An entrepreneur bears the risk of bringing a new product or service to market.

Entrepreneur.q: Which person is best described as an entrepreneur?
Entrepreneur.right: A student who starts a bike-repair service
wrong: An employee who receives a bonus for meeting this year's sales target at work
Entrepreneur.exp: Starting a new business and bearing its risk.

Entrepreneur motivations.q: Jordan loves fixing bikes and sees students struggling to get repairs. Which motivations fit?
wrong: Only profit, since entrepreneurs never start businesses for any other reason
Entrepreneur motivations.exp: Motivations include profit, problem-solving and passion.

Entrepreneur motivations.q: Which is NOT one of the three motivations in your study guide?
wrong: Solving a problem that customers have and are frustrated by every day
Entrepreneur motivations.exp: Profit, problem-solving and passion; nothing is guaranteed.

Idea generation.q: Lena watches families struggling to carry gear at tournaments and interviews parents. What is she doing?
Idea generation.right: Generating ideas by observing and interviewing
wrong: Building a minimum viable product to test whether parents will buy her backpack
Idea generation.exp: Ideas come from observing, interviewing and surveying.

Idea generation.q: Which method fits idea generation in your study guide?
wrong: Signing an exclusive agreement with the only supplier of a special material

Design thinking.q: Which order matches design thinking in your study guide?
Design thinking.right: Validate, develop the solution, build an MVP
wrong: Build the final product, then launch it, then ask customers what they think
Design thinking.exp: Validation (test, feedback, iterate) → solution development → MVP.

Design thinking.q: Why does design thinking start by testing ideas with customers?
Design thinking.right: To avoid building something customers don't want
wrong: To make sure the product is as expensive as possible before it reaches stores
Design thinking.exp: Testing first saves time and money.

Validation.q: Before buying equipment, Jordan surveys 200 students about a repair plan. Which step is this?
wrong: Launch, since Jordan is now selling repair plans to students on campus
Validation.exp: Testing an idea with customers before committing resources is validation.

Validation.q: Maya runs a mobile grooming van before renting a storefront. What does this show?
Validation.right: Validating the model before a big commitment
wrong: Creating a barrier to entry so that other groomers can't compete with her
Validation.exp: She tests demand before a large financial commitment.

Iteration.q: Lena redesigns the straps and enlarges a compartment after families test her backpack. What is this?
wrong: Mass production, because she is preparing to manufacture hundreds of backpacks
This step is improving the design.
Iteration.exp: Repeated improvements from feedback are iteration.

Iteration.q: Why do businesses iterate on products?
Iteration.right: Each round of feedback improves the product
wrong: Iteration guarantees that the product will never fail once it is launched
Iteration.exp: Iteration means improving repeatedly based on testing and feedback.

MVP hierarchy.q: An MVP looks great but often crashes. Which requirement has it failed?
wrong: Engaging, because users get bored when the app keeps crashing on them
MVP hierarchy.exp: Your guide's order: functional, reliable, usable, engaging.

MVP hierarchy.q: Which must an MVP achieve FIRST?
MVP hierarchy.right: Functional: it works and solves the core problem
wrong: Engaging: it has unique value that keeps users coming back again and again

Keep it simple.q: Why might a founder test a rough, unpolished prototype?
Keep it simple.right: Rough versions get more honest feedback
wrong: Rough prototypes are always cheaper to sell in stores than finished products
Keep it simple.exp: Keep it simple: unpolished prototypes draw honest feedback.

Keep it simple.q: Which action fits the "keep it simple" principle?
Keep it simple.right: Testing a cardboard model before building the real thing
wrong: Spending a year perfecting every detail before letting anyone see the product
Keep it simple.exp: Simple prototypes give quick, honest feedback.

Embrace friction.q: Why does your study guide say to embrace friction early?
Embrace friction.right: Early failures cost less than failures at scale
wrong: Friction always means the idea should be abandoned immediately and forgotten
Embrace friction.exp: Early failures save time and money later.

Embrace friction.q: A prototype fails a test in week one. Under "embrace friction," how should the team see it?
Embrace friction.right: A cheap lesson to fix before scaling
wrong: Proof that the business can never succeed and should close right away

User-centricity.q: A founder adds features he likes but users never asked for. Which principle is he ignoring?
wrong: Embrace friction, because he is making the product harder for users to learn
The issue is ignoring user needs.
Related, but the core issue is users.

User-centricity.right: Redesigning based on what users say they need
wrong: Choosing features based on what the company's engineers find most interesting
User-centricity.exp: User-centricity designs around real user needs.

Core values.q: A tech firm turns down a profitable project because it would collect user data aggressively, against its belief in privacy. What guided the decision?
wrong: Core competencies, because the firm is very good at protecting users' private data
The decision rests on a belief, not a skill.
Core values.exp: Beliefs like privacy are core values.

Core values.q: A company refuses to build a back door into its phones for law enforcement. This most reflects:
wrong: A core competency in low-cost manufacturing that lets it sell phones cheaply
Core values.exp: Core values guide strategic decisions (your slides: Apple and privacy).

Company culture.q: New employees quickly learn that everyone helps customers beyond what's required. What does this describe?
wrong: A code of conduct, since the company has written rules for helping customers
Nothing is written; it's shared behavior.
Company culture.exp: Shared values and behaviors are company culture.

Company culture.q: Why do businesses share their core values with employees?
Company culture.right: To build a culture where everyone works toward the same goals
wrong: To meet a legal requirement that all businesses must publish their values
Company culture.exp: Shared values align employees and shape culture.

Core competencies.q: Schools buy Spark Robotics' kits mainly for its lesson plans and live teacher support, not the hardware. What is its core competency?
wrong: Producing robotics kits at a lower cost than any other company in the market
Core competencies.exp: Core competencies are the capabilities that let a firm outperform rivals.

Core competencies.q: Spark Robotics wants to expand to high schools. Which question matters most?
Core competencies.right: Will its teacher support create value there too?
wrong: Can the company lower its manufacturing costs without lowering the quality of its kits?
Will high schools buy more kits?
Core competencies.exp: Businesses weigh their core competencies when choosing opportunities.

Vision statement.q: "To become the most trusted provider of healthy school meals in the state." What is this?
wrong: A mission statement, because it says what the company does for its customers
It states an aspiration: where it wants to go.
It's not about why to choose a product.
Vision statement.exp: A vision statement describes where the business aspires to go.

Vision statement.q: Which proposal best supports a vision "to become the most trusted provider of healthy school meals in the state"?
Vision statement.right: Independent nutrition certification and gradual expansion
wrong: Cutting prices and using standardized menus to win contracts in as many districts as possible
Trust and health matter more than speed and price here.
Expanding fast while keeping current standards
Vision statement.exp: Choose the option that builds trust and reaches the state.

Mission statement.q: "We prepare affordable, nutritious meals that help students learn and thrive every day." What is this?
wrong: A vision statement, because it describes the company's hopes for its students' futures
It says what the company does and how.
Mission statement.exp: A mission statement says what a business does and how.

Mission statement.q: A prosthetics maker's site says: "using recycled materials and 3D printing to provide affordable devices to underserved communities." What is this?
wrong: A vision statement, since it describes the future the company hopes to create
It explains what it does and how.

For-profit business.q: Which organization is a for-profit business?
wrong: The American Red Cross, which provides disaster relief around the world
For-profit business.exp: For-profits aim to earn profit for owners.

For-profit business.q: How can a for-profit business increase its profit?
wrong: Reinvest every dollar of surplus back into its programs, as the law requires

Social enterprise.q: TOMS gives part of its profits to social causes while selling shoes for profit. What kind of organization is it?
wrong: A nonprofit, because it gives money to charities that work on social issues
Social enterprise.exp: Profit plus social or environmental goals: social enterprise.

Social enterprise.q: A prosthetics company charges a "fair price" that covers costs and modest growth instead of the highest price possible. This reflects:
Social enterprise.right: Its core values meeting the market price
wrong: A desire for a monopoly combined with buyers who want the lowest possible price
Social enterprise.exp: A social enterprise's beliefs shape how it prices.

Nonprofit organization.q: What is a key difference between a nonprofit and a traditional business?
wrong: Nonprofits are not allowed to have mission statements or vision statements
Traditional businesses serve the public good only
Nonprofit organization.exp: By law, a nonprofit's surplus goes back into the organization.

Nonprofit organization.q: Where does a nonprofit usually get much of its money?
wrong: Selling shares of stock to investors who expect to receive part of the profits
Nonprofit organization.exp: Nonprofits rely on donations, grants and fundraising.

Unethical behavior.q: A founder wants to advertise a filter as "clinically proven" with no testing done. Why is this the biggest ethical concern?
Unethical behavior.right: It makes claims with no reliable evidence
wrong: Applying for a patent before production starts is a form of unfair competition
Unethical behavior.exp: Unsupported claims are deceptive, a form of unethical behavior.

Unethical behavior.q: Which is an example of unethical behavior from your study guide?
wrong: Hiring an outside accounting firm to prepare the company's tax documents each year
Unethical behavior.exp: Falsifying, misusing property, concealing data and fraud.

Incentive structures.q: A company pays big bonuses for hitting sales targets no matter how. Some reps start lying to customers. What is the root cause?
wrong: A strong code of conduct that employees must follow at all times
Incentive structures.exp: Poor incentives can push employees toward unethical choices.

Incentive structures.q: Which change would best fix incentives that reward results "at any cost"?
Incentive structures.right: Reward both results and honest methods
wrong: Raise the bonus for hitting targets so employees are even more motivated to sell
Incentive structures.exp: Incentives should not push people toward unethical choices.

Ethical dilemma.q: A thermostat has a minor Wi-Fi bug; fixing it delays launch four months and costs $8 million. Executives weigh customers, shareholders and reputation. What is this?
Ethical dilemma.right: An ethical dilemma involving competing responsibilities
wrong: A conflict between two market segments that want different thermostat features
Ethical dilemma.exp: Competing responsibilities with no clearly right option.

Ethical dilemma.q: What makes a situation an ethical dilemma rather than a simple wrong?
Ethical dilemma.right: No option is clearly right or wrong
wrong: Breaking a law that clearly protects customers from unsafe products

Code of conduct.q: A company publishes written rules for how employees handle gifts from suppliers. What is this?
wrong: A mission statement that explains what the company does and how it does it

Code of conduct.q: A code of conduct mainly helps by:
Code of conduct.right: Making expected behavior clear in writing
wrong: Guaranteeing that no employee will ever make an unethical choice at work

Ethics training.q: A bank holds yearly workshops where staff practice handling fraud situations. What is this?
wrong: Accountability, since employees who commit fraud will be fired by the bank
Ethics training.exp: Ongoing programs that build ethical skills.

Ethics training.q: Why is ethics training ongoing rather than one-time?
Ethics training.right: New situations and employees keep coming
wrong: The law requires companies to retrain every employee every single week

Accountability.q: A manager who falsified reports loses a promotion and must repay bonuses. What does this show?
wrong: A strong incentive structure that rewards managers for reporting results quickly
Accountability.exp: Internal repercussions for wrongdoing are accountability.

wrong: Employees who break the code of conduct are disciplined by their managers

Ethical leadership.q: A CEO publicly refuses an expensive gift from a supplier, following the same rule as staff. What does this show?
wrong: Outsourcing the company's decisions to the supplier's leadership team
Ethical leadership.exp: Executives model the behavior they expect.

Ethical leadership.q: Why does ethical leadership matter so much?
Ethical leadership.right: Employees follow what leaders actually do
wrong: Leaders are the only people in a company who can behave unethically
It replaces the code of conduct

Internal stakeholders.q: Which group is an internal stakeholder?
wrong: Customers who buy the company's products at stores across the country
Internal stakeholders.exp: Internal stakeholders work inside the business.

Internal stakeholders.q: Factory workers would be affected by a plan to automate production. As stakeholders they are:
wrong: External, because they would lose their jobs and leave the company afterward
They are inside the business now.

External stakeholders.q: A thermostat launches without disclosing a bug. Which stakeholder is most directly affected first?
wrong: Shareholders who expect higher profits from the company this quarter
External stakeholders.exp: Customers, external stakeholders, feel it first.

External stakeholders.q: Which group is an external stakeholder?
wrong: Managers who oversee the company's day-to-day operations and its employees
External stakeholders.exp: Customers, community, investors and suppliers are external.

Net benefit framework.q: A device maker can't tell if delaying a launch is right or wrong. Which approach best helps decide?
Net benefit framework.right: Greatest total benefit, least total harm
wrong: Pick whatever produces the biggest short-term return for the investors

Net benefit framework.q: A company launches while clearly telling hospitals about a software issue and sending a fix soon. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
Net benefit framework.right: It balances interests while increasing transparency
wrong: It removes every possible ethical concern because hospitals got advance notice
Net benefit framework.exp: A balanced choice across stakeholders, with transparency.

Strategic alignment framework.q: A company known for "radical honesty" chooses to publicly disclose a product flaw. Which framework fits best?
wrong: Net benefit, because disclosure always produces the most good for everyone
The reason given is fit with values.
The stated reason is its values.
Strategic alignment framework.exp: Choosing what fits stated values is strategic alignment.

Strategic alignment framework.q: Which question applies the strategic alignment framework?
Strategic alignment framework.right: Does this match our stated values?
wrong: Which option produces the greatest total benefit for every group affected?
How will the public see us?
Strategic alignment framework.exp: Strategic alignment checks fit with values and mission.

Reputation framework.q: A firm recalls a product early because news coverage could destroy trust in the brand. Which framework is it using?
wrong: Strategic alignment, since the recall fits the company's mission statement
The stated reason is public trust.
Reputation framework.exp: Protecting public standing is the reputation framework.

Reputation framework.q: Why might the reputation framework favor honesty even when it's costly?
Reputation framework.right: Lost trust can cost more over time
wrong: Honest companies are always exempt from lawsuits and government fines

Liability.right: Who must pay if the business can't pay its debts?
wrong: Which department in the company is responsible for hiring new employees?
Liability.exp: Liability is legal responsibility for a business's debts and losses.

Liability.q: Why do growing businesses often change their structure?
Liability.right: To reduce risk or raise money
wrong: To avoid having to pay any taxes to the government ever again
Liability.exp: Structure affects control, liability and access to funding.

Unlimited liability.q: A sole proprietor's bakery fails owing $50,000. What can creditors pursue?
Unlimited liability.right: The owner's personal savings and property
wrong: Only the bakery's equipment, since the owner's own property is legally protected
Unlimited liability.exp: With unlimited liability, personal assets can pay business debts.

Unlimited liability.q: Which structures usually have unlimited liability?
wrong: LLCs and corporations, because their owners are responsible for every decision
Unlimited liability.exp: Owners of these structures are usually personally responsible.

Limited liability.q: An LLC owner invested $20,000 and the business fails owing $100,000. What can she lose?
wrong: Her house, car and savings, since she owns the business that owes the money
Limited liability.exp: Limited liability: owners lose only what they invested.

Limited liability.q: Kai and Nora's partnership is growing. Which reason best justifies switching to an LLC?
wrong: To hire more marketing employees for the new advertising campaign this year

Sole proprietorship.q: Olivia starts a home invitation business with low costs and wants full control. Which factor most likely led her to choose a sole proprietorship?
Sole proprietorship.right: Low startup costs and being the only owner
wrong: Expecting to need outside investment to support rapid growth next year
Sole proprietorship.exp: Sole proprietorships fit one owner with low startup costs.

Sole proprietorship.q: A year later Olivia signs large contracts with penalties for late delivery. Why might she reconsider her structure?
Sole proprietorship.right: Her personal financial risk has grown
wrong: Her invitation product line has expanded to include more paper designs
Sole proprietorship.exp: Bigger risks make limited liability more attractive.

Partnership.q: Kai buys beans and roasts; Nora handles café clients and the website. They share profits. What is their structure?
wrong: A corporation, because they divide the company's work into separate departments
Partnership.exp: Two or more owners sharing control and profits.

Partnership.q: Why are partnerships often harder to end than sole proprietorships?
Partnership.right: Ending one needs the partners' agreement
wrong: The government must approve every partnership's closing in a public hearing

Limited liability company (LLC).q: Which feature is true of an LLC?
Limited liability company (LLC).right: It can attract investors but cannot sell stock
wrong: It must be run by a board of directors elected by many public shareholders
It can have only one owner
Limited liability company (LLC).exp: LLCs offer limited liability, flexible management and moderate funding.

Limited liability company (LLC).q: Why do many owners choose an LLC over a corporation?
wrong: LLCs have the greatest access to funding because they sell shares of stock
Limited liability company (LLC).exp: Limited liability with flexible, simpler management.

Corporation.q: Sara turns her delivery business into a corporation to buy a fleet of electric vans. What did she gain?
wrong: Total control over every daily decision in each of the company's departments
Corporation.exp: Corporations can raise capital by selling stock.

Corporation.q: What trade-off would Olivia face if she organized as a corporation?
Corporation.right: More funding, but giving up sole control
wrong: Lower startup costs, but losing the personal protection she has right now
Complete control, but full personal liability
Corporation.exp: Owners cede control to shareholders and a board.

C-corporation.q: Which feature belongs to a C-corporation?
wrong: Pass-through taxation, with profits taxed only once on the owners' returns
C-corporation.exp: Your study guide: C-corps face double taxation.

C-corporation.q: A company wants to raise as much capital as possible from many investors. Which structure fits best?
wrong: Sole proprietorship, since one owner can make funding decisions more quickly
C-corporation.exp: C-corporations have the greatest capital access.

S-corporation.q: Which is true of an S-corporation?
wrong: Unlimited shareholders and double taxation on every dollar the company earns
S-corporation.exp: S-corps pass profits through and cap shareholders at 100.

S-corporation.q: A company expects to grow to 300 shareholders. Why wouldn't an S-corporation work?
wrong: S-corps can't have limited liability for any of their shareholders at all

Board of directors.q: After reviewing an expansion proposal, the board approves it. What role is the board playing?
wrong: Managing daily operations and setting the tutoring schedules for each location
Board of directors.exp: The board oversees major strategic decisions on behalf of shareholders.

Board of directors.q: Who elects a corporation's board of directors?
wrong: The CEO, who chooses the board members to help run the company each day

Executives.q: A company must decide whether it can afford a $2 million expansion. Who is most responsible?
wrong: The CEO, since the CEO makes every decision in the company personally
Finance questions go to the CFO.
Executives.exp: The Chief Financial Officer oversees financial decisions.

Executives.q: In a corporation, to whom do executives like the CEO report?
wrong: The department managers, who supervise the executives on behalf of employees
Executives.exp: Executives report to the board and shareholders.

Outsourcing.q: A coffee roaster hires an outside firm to prepare its financial statements so the owners can focus on growth. Why?
wrong: To gain control of every stage of its supply chain from farm to café
Outsourcing.exp: Outsourcing taps specialized skills and frees owners to focus.

Outsourcing.q: A board suggests paying a tech company to store the firm's data instead of running its own servers. What is this?
wrong: Vertical integration, because the company is adding a new stage to its business
It's handing a task to another firm.
Outsourcing.exp: Paying another firm for a function is outsourcing.

Sales and marketing.q: As a coffee business grows, which task would most likely go to Nora, who handles clients and advertising?
Sales and marketing.right: Analyzing survey data to find a new target market
wrong: Forecasting the company's cash flow for the next quarter of the year
Sales and marketing.exp: Finding customers is sales and marketing.

Sales and marketing.q: After sales decline, a company weighs more advertising versus a redesign. Your slides assign this to:
wrong: Accounting, because the department records all of the company's sales figures
Sales and marketing.exp: Your slides list this decision under sales and marketing.

Research and development (R&D).q: Competitors keep releasing bottles with new features. Which reason best justifies giving R&D more money?
wrong: Production delays have raised the company's shipping and transportation costs
Research and development (R&D).exp: R&D designs new products to stay competitive.

Research and development (R&D).q: A firm designs and tests an improved version of an existing product. Which department?
wrong: Operations, since the improved product will eventually be produced in the factory
Research and development (R&D).exp: R&D improves goods, services and processes.

Operations.q: A bottle company invests in R&D but not operations, and retailers cut orders because deliveries stay late. What does this show?
wrong: Customer surveys found demand for additional bottle features, so R&D was right
Operations.exp: Operations handles on-time production and delivery.

Operations.q: A company schedules workers and manages production of goods. Which department?
wrong: Human resources, because the department manages the company's workers

Accounting.q: A company records revenues and expenses and prepares financial statements. Which department?
wrong: Finance, because the department deals with the company's money every day
Accounting.exp: Accounting records transactions and prepares statements.

Accounting.q: How do accounting and finance differ?
Accounting.right: Accounting records; finance plans and allocates
wrong: Accounting decides whether to borrow money; finance records all the transactions
Accounting.exp: Accounting tracks; finance budgets, invests and borrows.

Finance.q: A department analyzes electricity versus fuel costs and secures a multimillion-dollar loan for new vans. Which is it?
wrong: Operations, since the vans will be used every day to make the deliveries
Finance.exp: Finance manages funds, borrowing and investment.

Finance.q: A company evaluates whether to borrow money or invest in new equipment. Which department?
wrong: R&D, since new equipment helps the company design better products in the future

Human resources (HR).q: A tutoring company must hire 75 online tutors before school starts. Which department leads?
wrong: Operations, because the tutors will deliver the company's main service to students
Human resources (HR).exp: HR recruits, hires and trains employees.

Human resources (HR).q: A company builds a long-term plan to recruit, train and retain skilled workers. Which department?
wrong: Operations, since the workers will run the company's production lines

Artisan production.q: Candles are poured, decorated and inspected by hand, and customers wait three weeks. Which process is this?
wrong: Mass production, since the company makes many candles for customers every month
Hand work with long waits is artisan.
Artisan production.exp: Skilled hand labor, small quantities, unique items.

Artisan production.q: Before automating, what should a handmade-candle maker consider most?
Artisan production.right: Whether customers value handmade quality enough
wrong: Whether competitors will lower their prices after the company automates production
Whether wax suppliers will cut prices
Artisan production.exp: Its differentiation may depend on being handmade.

Mass production.q: A candle maker buys equipment that makes thousands of identical candles a week. Most likely outcome?
wrong: Customers will automatically see the candles as being higher quality than before
Mass production.exp: Mass production raises output but may weaken a handmade identity.

Mass production.q: Why is mass production more than "making cheap stuff"?
Mass production.right: It's a strategic choice that lowers cost per unit
wrong: It always produces the highest-quality goods available anywhere in the market
It removes the need for a supply chain
Mass production.exp: Mass production spreads costs and can create a barrier to entry.

Supply chain.q: Strawberries are harvested, stored cold, shipped to a distributor, then to grocery chains. What is the farm's role?
Supply chain.right: It creates the product before intermediaries move it
wrong: Its main job is transporting the strawberries to the grocery stores
Supply chain.exp: The farm is the origin; distributors and retailers follow.

Supply chain.q: Floods delay trucks carrying strawberries from warehouses. Who most likely runs out first?
wrong: The farm, because it will have to stop picking strawberries right away
Supply chain.exp: A break mid-chain empties retail shelves first.

wrong: A finished dining table that is ready to be shipped to a furniture store
Raw materials.exp: Raw materials are basic natural resources.

Raw materials.q: A drought cuts the cotton harvest. Which part of a T-shirt maker's supply chain is hit first?
wrong: The retailer, which sells T-shirts to customers in stores and online
Raw materials.exp: Cotton is a raw material at the start of the chain.

Suppliers.q: Ford buys steel, engines and tires from firms in several countries. Those firms are:
wrong: Retailers, because they sell their products to another company for money
Suppliers.exp: Suppliers provide raw materials or components.

Suppliers.q: What do businesses weigh when choosing suppliers?
wrong: Only the lowest price, because nothing else affects the final product
Suppliers.exp: Your slides list cost, quality, efficiency, convenience and reliability.

Manufacturers.q: Which stage turns parts into a finished car?
wrong: Distributors, which carry the parts between different countries around the world
Manufacturers.exp: Manufacturers transform inputs into finished goods.

Manufacturers.q: Quality control mostly takes place at which stage?
wrong: Retail, where store employees check products before customers buy them
Manufacturers.exp: Manufacturing involves machinery, labor, assembly and quality control.

Distributors.q: A company carries finished goods from factories to regional hubs. It is a:
wrong: Manufacturer, since it handles products that came from the company's factories

Distributors.q: A national distributor combines shipments from many farms and delivers to grocery chains. Why use one?
Distributors.right: It moves goods from many producers efficiently
wrong: It grows the strawberries more cheaply than any individual farm could

Wholesaler.q: A business buys snacks in bulk from manufacturers and resells them to corner stores. It is a:
wrong: Retailer, because it sells the snacks to other businesses for a profit
Wholesaler.exp: Wholesalers buy in bulk and resell to retailers.

Wholesaler.q: Why might a small store buy from a wholesaler instead of the manufacturer?
Wholesaler.right: It can buy smaller amounts from one source
wrong: Wholesalers always sell products at a lower price than manufacturers charge

Retailers.q: Which is the final link in the supply chain?
wrong: Wholesalers, since they sell products to the stores that customers visit
Mining raw materials and turning them into the parts that factories need
Retailers.exp: Your slides list merchandising, inventory and customer service.

Logistics.q: A company plans how goods and information move from its factory to customers. What is this?
wrong: Merchandising, since it decides how the products will look on the store shelves
Logistics.exp: Logistics plans and manages movement of goods and information.

Logistics.q: How can efficient logistics create a low-price advantage?
Logistics.right: It cuts the cost of moving goods
wrong: It allows the company to raise prices because the products arrive faster
Logistics.exp: Low-price supply chains use cheaper resources, mass production and efficient logistics.

Merchandising.q: A store moves a new snack to eye level with a bright sign and a sale price. What is this?
wrong: Logistics, because the store is moving products to a different shelf location
Merchandising.exp: Merchandising is how products are displayed, arranged, priced and promoted.

Merchandising.q: Why do big brands pay for eye-level shelf space?
wrong: Eye-level products are legally protected from all competition in the store
Merchandising.exp: Merchandising affects what customers notice and buy.

Inventory.q: A store keeps 200 bikes on hand to sell. What is this stock called?
wrong: Merchandising, since the bikes are arranged on display for customers to see
Inventory.exp: Inventory is the stock a business keeps to sell.

Inventory.q: Why must retailers manage inventory carefully?
Inventory.right: To avoid shortages and excess stock
wrong: Because carrying more inventory always increases a store's profits
Inventory.exp: Too little causes stockouts; too much ties up money.

Stockout.q: Demand for candles keeps exceeding what the company can make. Which problem is most likely?
wrong: Increased product differentiation that sets the candles apart from competitors
Stockout.exp: When demand exceeds supply, inventory runs out.

Stockout.q: What is the usual result of a stockout?
wrong: Higher profits, since the store doesn't have to pay to store any products
Stockout.exp: Stockouts mean orders can't be filled.

Low-price leadership.q: A company uses mass production, economies of scale and process optimization. Which strategy?
wrong: High-quality differentiation, since its efficient processes produce better products
A pricing tactic, not a supply chain strategy.
Low-price leadership.exp: Mass production and efficiency support low prices.

Low-price leadership.q: Which company best fits low-price leadership?
Low-price leadership.right: A discount store with huge volume and lean operations
wrong: A watchmaker using rare metals and hand-assembly for each piece it sells
Low-price leadership.exp: Scale and efficiency drive low prices.

High-quality differentiation.q: A laptop maker sources premium liquid-cooling parts to have the fastest machines. Which strategy?
wrong: Low-price leadership, since faster machines help the company sell more laptops
High-quality differentiation.exp: Premium resources and precision support differentiation.

High-quality differentiation.q: Which supply chain choice fits high-quality differentiation?
High-quality differentiation.right: Paying more for durable premium materials
wrong: Switching to the cheapest available materials to cut the price of each product

Supply chain risks.q: A laptop maker's shipping costs from South Korea rise due to new rules on cargo ships. This is:
wrong: A strength of its mass-production process, which lowers the cost of each laptop
It's a risk, not a strength.
Supply chain risks.exp: External changes that raise costs or delay delivery are supply chain risks.

Supply chain risks.q: Which is most likely to delay deliveries and threaten a firm's advantage?
Supply chain risks.right: Political instability where materials are sourced
wrong: Rising household incomes in the local market where the company sells products
Supply chain risks.exp: Political instability is a supply chain risk.

Scaling operations.q: A laptop maker moves from hand-assembly to automated lines and its cost per unit falls. What did it do?
wrong: Moved toward an artisan process in order to offer customers more customization
Scaling operations.exp: Scaling expands capacity while improving efficiency.

Scaling operations.q: How can scaling create a barrier to entry?
Scaling operations.right: New firms can't match the low costs
wrong: It makes the government stop new firms from entering the market legally
Scaling operations.exp: Newcomers lack the scale to match established costs.

Economies of scale.q: Why does producing 1 million units often cost less per unit than producing 1,000?
Economies of scale.right: Fixed costs are spread over more units
wrong: Workers are paid less per hour when the factory makes a larger number of units
Economies of scale.exp: Spreading fixed costs lowers cost per unit.

Economies of scale.q: A large chain and a single shop sell the same product. Rising ingredient costs hurt the shop more. Why?
Economies of scale.right: The chain buys in volume and spreads costs
wrong: The single shop pays a special tax that only small businesses have to pay
Economies of scale.exp: Scale gives large firms cost advantages.

Exclusive agreements.q: A laptop maker signs a 3-year deal stopping its cooling supplier from selling to rivals. What does this create?
wrong: Lower quality, since the supplier will stop improving its cooling systems
A switch to a service model
Exclusive agreements.exp: Exclusive agreements limit rivals' access to key parts.

Exclusive agreements.q: Why might a new rival struggle when an established firm has exclusive supplier contracts?
Exclusive agreements.right: It can't get the parts it needs
wrong: It lacks problem-solution fit because customers don't want the product
It didn't write a mission statement

Restrictive distribution.q: A soda giant pushes stores to keep rival drinks off its coolers. Which barrier is this?
wrong: An exclusive agreement with suppliers, since it controls who makes the soda
Restrictive distribution.exp: Limiting which retailers carry rivals is restrictive distribution.

Restrictive distribution.q: How does restrictive distribution hurt a new brand?
Restrictive distribution.right: It can't reach customers through stores
wrong: It raises the new brand's production costs by making materials more expensive
It gives the brand a patent
Restrictive distribution.exp: Blocked retail access keeps rivals off shelves.

Globalization.q: Students check clothing labels and find items made in Vietnam, Bangladesh and Mexico. What does this show?
wrong: Vertical integration, because one company made every item from start to finish
Globalization.exp: Goods made worldwide reflect global connections.

Globalization.q: Why does Ford use a global supply chain?
Globalization.right: Different regions make certain parts cheaper or better
wrong: The law requires automakers to buy every part from a different country
Globalization.exp: Specialization lowers costs and improves access to inputs.

Globalization trade-offs.q: Which is a disadvantage of globalization?
Globalization trade-offs.right: Job losses in industries that can't compete with imports
wrong: A wider variety of goods and services available to consumers at home

Globalization trade-offs.q: Why can globalization make supply chains fragile?
Globalization trade-offs.right: Countries depend on each other for inputs
wrong: Because global trade is illegal in most countries and can be stopped at any time
Globalization trade-offs.exp: Interdependence means one disruption can spread.
